To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) SPMs that account for the spatial structure of the population are more accurate than SPMs that do not account for the spatial distribution, and (2) monitoring of the stock within a no-take marine protected area is essential for conducting an accurate stock assessment

spatially explicit surplus production models performed better than spatially aggregated surplus production models in assessing populations with marine protected areas, and that the accuracy of surplus production models improved as the percentage of the population in the marine protected area increased.

spatially explicit surplus production models perform better than spatially aggregated surplus production models, that the accuracy of surplus production models improves as MPA size increases except under the scenario in which no index of abundance is available in the MPA, and that monitoring of the stock within a marine protected area is essential for conducting an accurate stock assessment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accuracy of stock assessment methods when applied to a stock with part of its range protected from fishing by an MPA.
the effects of a no-take marine protected area on the accuracy of surplus production models.
the effect of MPAs on stock assessments, which is a topic of interest in the field of marine fisheries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the accuracy of SPM stock assessments is affected by the presence of an MPA.
SPMs can be accurate in areas with MPA if there is a reliable index of abundance available within the MPA.
spatially explicit SSMs can be used to estimate stock abundance and fishing mortality in areas with MPAS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of MP As on stock assessments depend strongly on the size of the MPA and the rate of migration between MP A and non-MPA areas.
the spatially explicit SSMs are the preferred method for stock assessment when an MPA is present in the stock.
MPAs have a large effect on the accuracy of SPMs and the accuracy of assessments increases as the MPA size increases, but only if the index of abundance within an MPA can be monitored.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spatially aggregated SPSMs are likely to provide inaccurate estimates of stock status and abundance in populations with MPAs.
spatially explicit SSMs are needed to accurately assess populations with MPAs.
the effects of MPA implementation on stock assessment results depend on the spatial configuration of the MPA and on the level of migration among MPA and non- MPA regions.
